name: LATVIA

flag.title: Latvian Flag
flag.note: Dark carmine red — white — carmine red

lead: Latvia is a small Baltic country where half the land is ancient forest. Singing is a national sport. Storks nest on chimneys, amber washes up on beaches, and Midsummer bonfires burn till sunrise.
geo: Latvia is flat and low, with no point above 312 metres. More than half the land is ancient forest of pine, birch, and oak. Boggy marshes are full of dragonflies.
The Daugava River flows west to the sea at Riga. The Baltic shoreline has 500 km of sandy beach. After storms, you can find golden amber there.
animals: Brown bears, grey wolves, lynx, and moose live in Latvia's forests. The moose is Europe's largest deer. Bison and wild horses roam the dunes at Pape Nature Reserve.
Around 14,000 pairs of white storks nest in Latvia, perching on chimneys. The national bird is the cheerful little white wagtail.
culture: Latvians have collected over 1.2 million folk-song texts called dainas. Every five years, the Song and Dance Festival fills Riga with 40,000 performers.
Latvians eat dark rye bread at every meal. On Midsummer Night, families light bonfires and weave flower crowns. Everyone hunts for the fern flower, which does not exist.
history: Latvians traded Baltic amber with ancient Rome. In the 13th century, German crusading knights built stone castles and ruled for centuries. Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918.
The Soviets occupied Latvia in 1940 and again from 1944. Latvia restored full independence on 21 August 1991.
wows: Riga has 800+ Art Nouveau buildings, more than Paris or Barcelona.
Riga says it raised the world's first Christmas tree in 1510.
Latvia has 1.2 million folk-song texts, more per person than almost anywhere.
The 1989 Baltic Way was the longest human chain ever, at 675 km.
Around 40,000 people sing in one huge choir every five years.
More than 55% of Latvia is forest.
Each spring, about 14,000 stork pairs fly back from Africa to nest here.

myths.myth: All Baltic countries speak one language
myths.fact: Estonian is close to Finnish. Latvian and Lithuanian are cousins, but speakers still cannot understand each other.
Bogs soak up carbon and store it. Their sour mud keeps old wood and tools from rotting.
